title: Voltage
summary: Voltage is the electrical pressure that pushes current around a circuit — measured in volts. A 9 V battery pushes twice as hard as a 4.5 V one, and the voltmeter shows the push waiting at the battery's ends. In this model you stack 1.5 V cells: double the push, double the current the bulb sees.

processes: Metering the volts at the terminals
plainLanguageExplanation: Voltage is the electrical pressure that pushes current around a circuit — the 'how hard' of electricity, measured in volts (V). Picture water: the battery is your water tower, the wire is the pipe, and current is the water flowing to your house. Voltage is the height of the tower — how hard the water pressure pushes. Raise the voltage and the pressure climbs, driving more current through the same wire at the same resistance. A 9 V battery pushes twice as hard as a 4.5 V one. In this model you can see a battery bank holding small 1.5 V cells: tap to add the next cell, watch the voltmeter climb, and see the extra push force more current into the waiting bulb. That's why lights get brighter on bigger batteries and why 'volts' matter on every charger — the push decides the ride.

whyItMatters: Voltage is the pressure that makes circuits run, and its level decides battery life, bulb brightness, and which charger reaches a phone. Car batteries run at 12 V, mains at 120-230 V, and every LED strip names its working volts — understanding the push is the first step to making current do what you want.
didYouKnow: Household mains deliver about 230 V in many countries and about 120 V in North America — a difference you feel in appliance ratings. AAA, AA, and D cells all give 1.5 V yet carry different amounts of charge: volts tell the push, not the stamina.
